claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain and toughness in fusion plasma-facing structural materials are primarily governed by the evolution and stability of nanoscale precipitates.
Precipitate coarsening or loss of precipitate stability at high temperature enhances dislocation mobility through dynamic recovery mechanisms.
Enhanced dislocation mobility increases plastic-strain capacity and improves toughness.
The baseline material has a fine, well-distributed nanoscale precipitate dispersion and a high dislocation density produced by conventional thermomechanical processing.
A controlled heat treatment can induce precipitate coarsening, dissolution, or loss of precipitate stability in otherwise identical specimens.
Precipitate size, distribution, and stability determine how strongly precipitates obstruct dislocation motion.
Precipitate obstruction governs the interplay among dislocation glide, recovery, and grain-boundary processes.
At temperatures where dynamic recovery is active, stable fine precipitates restrict dislocation motion and limit plasticity.
Stable fine precipitates may confer brittleness under the proposed high-temperature conditions.
Coarsened or unstable precipitates are more easily bypassed by dislocations.
Easier precipitate bypass increases energy absorption before crack propagation.
Relative to the fine-precipitate baseline, precipitate-disrupted specimens will exhibit greater high-temperature plastic strain, ductility, and toughness.
The predicted improvements in plastic strain and toughness may be accompanied by reduced strength.
The hypothesis is limited to fusion-relevant alloys in which nanoscale precipitate strengthening is dominant, including advanced ferritic/martensitic steels or tungsten alloys.
The proposed mechanism is expected to operate approximately from 600 to 900 °C, where dynamic recovery and precipitate evolution are significant.
Grain-boundary character and radiation-induced defects may also affect plastic strain and toughness.
